extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, voters, and policymakers evaluating the proposed Constitution (readers of The Federalist Papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing principles and procedural provisions for the composition, size, selection, powers, and accountability of a representative legislative body under a federal constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative ratio / number of members
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative for every thirty thousand inhabitants will render the House both a safe and competent guardian of interests; the proposed proportion (one per 30,000) is adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison with Great Britain and with existing State practices is used to justify the ratio: Britain’s much larger constituent-to-representative ratios still preserved a valuable portion of freedom. After securing a sufficient number for safety, local information, and diffusive sympathy, further increase may be counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate number suffices because of state/local information
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws and local legislative proceedings supply much of the preparatory labor and information needed by a national legislature, so only a moderate number of federal representatives is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: within each State laws are largely uniform and available; representatives often will already possess local legislative experience, reducing the need for large federal delegations. This facilitates use of fewer but well-informed members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections as a principal restraint on representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Short and recurring terms (frequent elections) maintain representatives’ responsibility to the people and are the most effectual precaution against degeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent elections compel representatives to anticipate the review of their conduct and deter abuse of power; they are listed among multiple securities (duty, gratitude, interest, ambition) binding representatives to constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: No artificial qualifications for electors or eligibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors are to be the great body of the people; nothing in the federal plan permits a qualification of wealth, birth, religious faith, or civil profession to fetter the judgment or disappoint the inclination of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The electors are the same as those who elect corresponding state branches. This openness prevents systemic bias toward the rich, learned, or titled and supports broad popular choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and qualities of representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives will generally be distinguished by qualities which entitle them to preference (merit, virtue, wisdom) and thus be likely to serve faithfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they are chosen by fellow citizens, they are presumed to possess the attributes (esteem, competence) that recommend them; personal motives (pride, vanity, ambition) also bind them to maintain popular favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative self-application as a check
rubrics_metrics.description: The House can make no law which will not have its full operation on themselves and their friends, creating a strong bond between rulers and people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mutual application of laws is cited as one of the strongest bonds connecting those who govern with those governed, reducing the likelihood of legal discriminations favoring the few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of the purse as a check and instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The House’s exclusive control of supplies (the purse) is the most complete and effectual weapon for the representatives to obtain redress and carry into effect just measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example from British practice: control over money bills empowered representative bodies to enlarge their sphere of activity and check other branches; it also provides leverage to obtain reapportionments and augmentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive quorum or supermajority requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring more than a simple majority for a quorum or decisions would transfer power to the minority and reverse the fundamental principle that the majority should rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher thresholds could shield interested minorities, facilitate secessions, and obstruct measures needed for justice or the public good; ordinary majority rule is preferred to prevent minority domination and public convulsions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal assembly size — balance benefits and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: After securing a sufficient number for safety, local information, and diffusive sympathy with society, further enlargements of the assembly will counteract the people’s views and produce harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger assemblies increase the ascendancy of passion over reason, raise the proportion of limited-information members, and make the body more susceptible to eloquence and manipulation; thus there is a trade-off between representation breadth and deliberative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decennial census and reapportionment mechanism for augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A census every ten years is to readjust apportionment of representatives and to augment their number as population demands, with the single limitations that each State have at least one representative and that the whole number not exceed one per thirty thousand inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constitutional provisions create a periodic and institutionalized vehicle for adjusting representation as population changes; experience and state constitutions provide supporting precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral dynamics encourage augmentation where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Because one legislative branch represents citizens (favoring large states) and the other represents states (favoring small states), political incentives will typically support reasonable augmentations of representatives when large states demand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical politics: coalitions among larger states and senators from rapidly growing new states can be expected to facilitate reapportionment and augmentation despite occasional Senate opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: National legislature’s reserved power to regulate elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution grants Congress ultimate authority to make or alter regulations concerning the 'times, places, and manner' of elections (except places of choosing senators), on the ground that a government must contain means for its own preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretionary national authority is defended as necessary because no permanent election law could anticipate all future changes in the country's situation; placing ultimate power in the federal legislature is presented as constitutional prudence to preserve the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larger electorates reduce susceptibility to corruption and intrigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Electorates of five or six thousand citizens are more capable of choosing fit representatives and less liable to be corrupted by intrigues or bribes than electorates of five or six hundred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason and observed fact are invoked: larger numbers increase the likelihood of finding fit representatives and make diversion by private influence less effective; examples from states and cities are offered in support.
